title.instructions: Use a concise, task-focused workspace title of 3-7 words. Describe the Devsy change, fix, investigation, refactor, test, documentation update, or maintenance task. Include the repo issue number when one is provided and useful for identification. Avoid generic titles, filler words, random adjectives, animal names, whimsical names, or any other opaque generated naming.

branchName.instructions: Generate a descriptive lowercase kebab-case Git branch name that reflects the actual task. Use <type>/<issue-number>-<short-description> when the work is tied to a repo issue, otherwise use <type>/<short-description>. Choose a type from feat, fix, test, refactor, docs, chore, ci, build, or perf. Keep the description concise, specific, and understandable without additional context. Prefer examples such as fix/1223-docker-bind-create-src, feat/1211-workspace-down-alias, test/stabilize-podman-e2e, or chore/update-mise-toolchain. Never generate random, whimsical, adjective-animal, or otherwise opaque branch names.

commitMessage.instructions: Use Conventional Commits with a scope using the format <type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>. Use a lowercase Conventional Commit type such as feat, fix, test, refactor, docs, chore, ci, build, or perf. Choose the narrowest meaningful Devsy scope based on the code being changed. Common scopes include workspace, desktop, secrets, ssh, transport, docker, podman, e2e, ci, release, deps, mise, docs, provider, agent, tunnel, output, logging, updater, config, and auth. Use the imperative mood, keep the subject concise and specific, and do not end the subject with a period. Avoid generic messages such as 'update files', 'fix issue', or 'make changes'. Do not invent an unrelated scope when the repository component is clear.

pullRequest.instructions: Generate a Conventional Commit pull request title using <type>(<scope>): <concise summary>. The title should describe the primary user-visible or engineering change and should normally align with the dominant commit type and scope. Keep the pull request body concise and under 300 words. Include a '## Summary' section containing 2-5 bullets describing the concrete changes present in the diff. Include a '## Validation' section listing tests, linters, builds, static analysis, manual checks, or other verification that was actually performed. Never claim a validation step passed if it was not run. If validation could not be completed, explicitly state what could not be run and why. When the work resolves a GitHub issue, include an appropriate GitHub closing reference such as 'Fixes #123' or 'Closes #123'. Describe only changes actually present in the pull request. Avoid redundant background information, generic boilerplate, speculative claims, verbose implementation narratives, autogenerated filler, or release-note style marketing language.
